Among overseas property destinations for Indian buyers, Dubai used to be the most popular and often go-to choice. However, with Thailand and its relatively accessible prices, tourism-led rental demand and holiday home appeal, Phuket, particularly, is drawing Indian buyers.
According to Stuart Reading, managing director, Group Property Development at Banyan Group, “Indians are the fifth-largest buyers by value for Laguna Phuket, and they are the second-largest group of tourists in Phuket.” Banyan Group runs Laguna Phuket, a 1,000-acre integrated resort at Bang Tao with six hotels, a golf course and more than 3,000 branded residences.
He says that Thailand drew over 35 million visitors in 2025, and foreign buyers account for over 60% of Phuket’s condominium purchases.
“The core buyer is a high-net-worth individual or family office purchasing a legacy or trophy asset rather than a first home. It is often a second or third property bought for long-term capital preservation as much as lifestyle. We’re also seeing more second-home buyers relocating seasonally or working remotely from Phuket,” adds Reading.
According to Shiv Garg, director of Forteasia Realty Pvt. Ltd, a Delhi-based real estate developer, Thailand, particularly Phuket, is gaining traction as an alternative option rather than as a direct substitute for Dubai, largely due to its relatively lower property prices. Phuket is also perceived to offer greater capital appreciation potential. Around 80% of buyers in Phuket are purchasing second homes, compared with Dubai, where investment opportunities and visa-related benefits play a more prominent role.
“Three kinds of Indian buyers are driving interest: investors seeking geographic diversification and rental income, families buying holiday homes in places they visit often, and parents or professionals building an asset base where their children can study or work. Thailand suits them because it combines relatively accessible prices, tourism-driven rental demand, lifestyle appeal and proximity to India,” says Sanjay Chugh, city head and senior vice-president of Anarock Property Consultants Limited, an independent real estate services and advisory company in Mumbai.
Thailand also offers choice when it comes to property destinations. There is Bangkok for city buyers, Phuket for holiday-home seekers, and Pattaya for those on tighter budgets, says Anuj Goel, chairman of Pune-based Goel Ganga Developments.
Survey data, as Goel shares, indicates that approximately 13% of total wealth is now invested in international residential real estate, compared with around 5% a decade ago. This share is expected to increase over the long term.
Buyers generally fall within the 35-50 age group and include working professionals and entrepreneurs. Gen Z Indians, particularly those in their mid-20s to early 30s, are showing growing interest, especially in Dubai, as Goel rightly points out.
Dual-income, middle-income professionals are also increasingly exploring international real estate to benefit from higher rental yields and portfolio diversification.
Phuket is where that interest concentrates, and where prices reflect it. Reading says, “Land values along the west coast, particularly Bang Tao and neighbouring Layan, have climbed close to prime Bangkok levels, driven largely by how little beachfront is left. At Laguna Phuket, new beachfront homes start at about $3.5 million (approx. ₹32.5 crore) and run past $6 million (approx. ₹56 crore). Demand is strongest at the top of the range, where buyers want large, fully furnished, move-in-ready homes with branded services attached. Indian buyers, resident and non-resident, are among the fastest-growing groups, alongside Russians, Chinese and Kazakhs.”
According to Goel, there has been strong growth in international real estate investments from India. Approximately $528.7 million (approx ₹4,912 crore) was remitted overseas for real estate purchases in FY 2025-26, registering a 64% year-on-year increase. “The typical investment range is between $250,000 (approx ₹2.34 crore) and $1 million (approx ₹9.35 crore), with around 85% of people polled indicating an intention to invest within this bracket. Apartments and condominiums are the most popular property types, followed by villas and townhouses.”
The value of condominiums bought by Indians in Thailand rose 66.6% in the third quarter of 2026 from a year earlier, says Goel. Government data cited by Chugh shows Indians bought 237 condo units in 2025 at an average of about 6.9 million baht (roughly ₹1.9 crore), including some of the largest units among foreigners. That suggests Indians are not only buying compact investment flats; many want holiday homes and family assets. Chugh adds a caution: “I would distinguish between interest and actual purchasing capacity.”
Even though overseas property investment offers diversification, it also introduces risks that buyers may not encounter to the same extent in their domestic market. Currency fluctuations can affect returns: an investment may appreciate in local currency terms, but the return in Indian rupees could be lower if the foreign currency depreciates against the rupee. Currency appreciation, however, can also enhance returns.
“Failure to declare overseas assets in India can result in penalties. International real estate can also be less liquid than domestic property and other financial assets. Since restrictions on foreign ownership vary significantly across countries, investors must understand the applicable regulations before making a purchase,” Goel says.
Another consideration is the legal and regulatory framework governing foreign ownership. In Thailand, foreign nationals can own condominium units within the prescribed foreign ownership quota but cannot directly own the land. “For condominiums, both freehold and leasehold ownership are available to foreign buyers. Foreign freehold ownership is permitted up to 49% of the total condominium unit area, while other units can be purchased on a renewable leasehold basis,” says Reading.
On the Indian side, remittances above ₹10 lakh a year attract a 20% tax collected at source, creditable against final tax but tying up cash, and the property must be disclosed in the tax return. Chugh stresses that quoted yields are gross, not net. Vansh Jain, director of Global Partnerships, Petros Stone LLP, calls Thai condominiums “more of a lifestyle investment for Indian buyers”, warning that oversupply, management fees, a weak secondary market and taxes “can significantly reduce net returns compared with gross yields”. He says Thai property is better suited to investors with a horizon of 10 years or more who already hold a core portfolio in India. Currency matters as well: Garg says returns should be judged in rupees.
Buying property in Thailand may be more of a lifestyle decision than an investment. While relatively accessible prices and tourism-led rental demand may appeal to Indian buyers, actual returns depend on the location, ownership structure and costs of managing the property from afar. Thailand may offer an attractive overseas address, but buyers need to look beyond the appeal of owning a home abroad and assess whether the numbers add up.
The writer visited Laguna Phuket, Thailand, at the invitation of Banyan Group.
